subject: Economics
description: Banker to Government, currency issuance, FX manager, regulator, NABARD relationship

questions.stem: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was established under the RBI Act of:

options.option_text: 1947, the year of Indian independence
1934, taking over from the Imperial Bank of India
1955, after nationalisation of major banks
1969, the year fourteen banks were nationalised

questions.explanation: RBI Act, 1934. RBI began operations on 1 April 1935. Initially headquartered in Calcutta; HQ moved to Mumbai 1937. Originally privately owned; NATIONALISED on 1 January 1949 — wholly Government of India ownership since. Established on the recommendations of the Hilton Young Commission (1926). Central bank, currency authority, banker to government, regulator of commercial banks. Imperial Bank of India (founded 1921) was earlier the de facto central bank (and itself was nationalised in 1955 as the State Bank of India). Distractor 1 = independence year. Distractor 3 = SBI nationalisation year. Distractor 4 = 14 PSU banks nationalisation.

questions.stem: The RBI is the SOLE issuer of currency in India for denominations of:

options.option_text: All denominations including the one-rupee coins
All notes ₹2 and above (the ₹1 note is issued by Govt of India)
Only the higher denominations of ₹100 and above
Only currency notes; coins are issued by the SBI

questions.explanation: RBI issues notes ₹2 and ABOVE under the RBI Act 1934. The ₹1 note (and all coins) are issued by the GOVT OF INDIA under the Coinage Act, 2011 — though coins and the ₹1 note are CIRCULATED by RBI. Each Indian banknote bears the GOVERNOR's signature; the ₹1 note bears the FINANCE SECRETARY's signature. Banknotes printed at SPMCIL presses (Nashik, Dewas) and BRBNMPL presses (Mysore, Salboni). Coins minted at SPMCIL mints (Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Noida).

questions.stem: The RBI manages India's foreign-exchange reserves under which Act?

options.option_text: FERA (Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973)
FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999)
PMLA (Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002)
RBI Act, 1934, as the original parent statute

questions.explanation: FEMA, 1999 — replaced the older FERA (1973). FEMA is regulatory + facilitative; FERA was restrictive (criminal prosecution-based). India holds the 4th-largest FX reserves globally (~$700+ billion as of 2025), comprising foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs, IMF reserve position. RBI's reserve-management goals: liquidity, safety, return (in that order). Reserves provide an import cushion (~10-11 months of imports) and a buffer against currency volatility. PMLA — Enforcement Directorate's key statute, separate domain. RBI Act founded the bank but FX regulation came under FEMA later.

questions.stem: Which entity was carved OUT of the RBI in 1982 to focus on rural credit?

options.option_text: SIDBI, the Small Industries Development Bank of India
NABARD, the apex bank for agriculture and rural sectors
EXIM Bank, the Export-Import Bank of India for trade
NHB, the National Housing Bank for housing finance

questions.explanation: NABARD — established 12 July 1982, on the recommendations of the Sivaraman Committee. Took over the Agricultural Credit Department (ACD) and Rural Planning + Credit Cell (RPCC) from RBI. Functions: refinance facility for cooperative banks + RRBs, financial inclusion, supervision of cooperative + regional rural banks (RRBs). HQ Mumbai. Distractor 1 — SIDBI (1990) is for MSMEs. Distractor 3 — EXIM Bank (1982, separately) for export-import credit. Distractor 4 — NHB (1988) for housing finance, also created within RBI's framework.

questions.stem: The RBI is sometimes called the 'BANKER's BANK' because it:

options.option_text: Owns shares in commercial banks across the country
Holds banks' reserves and lends to them as lender of last resort
Issues commercial-bank ATM cards on behalf of those banks
Pays salaries of all the employees of commercial banks directly

questions.explanation: Banker's Bank functions: (1) HOLDS BANKS' RESERVES — every commercial bank maintains a CRR account with RBI (Cash Reserve Ratio of NDTL). (2) LENDER OF LAST RESORT — banks short of liquidity can borrow from RBI via repo / MSF / liquidity facilities. (3) CLEARING HOUSE — facilitates inter-bank settlements via NEFT/RTGS/IMPS. (4) Authority — RBI directs / regulates commercial banks under the Banking Regulation Act 1949. Distractor 1 — RBI doesn't generally hold shares; it regulates. Distractor 3 — false. Distractor 4 — false.

questions.stem: The Governor of RBI is appointed by:

options.option_text: The Lok Sabha by simple majority resolution
The Central Government, with a typical term of 3 years
The President in consultation with the CJI
The RBI's Central Board through internal election

questions.explanation: RBI Governor appointed by the Centre (effectively the Cabinet, on recommendation of the FSRASC — Financial Sector Regulatory Appointments Search Committee). Term — typically 3 years, extendable. Cannot exceed age 65 (general rule). Eminent Governors of RBI: C.D. Deshmukh (first Indian Governor, 1943-49), I.G. Patel, Manmohan Singh (1982-85), C. Rangarajan, Bimal Jalan, Y.V. Reddy, D. Subbarao, Raghuram Rajan (2013-16), Urjit Patel (2016-18), Shaktikanta Das (2018-24), Sanjay Malhotra (current, since Dec 2024). Distractor 1 — Lok Sabha doesn't vote on the Governor. Distractor 3 — CJI not involved. Distractor 4 — Central Board doesn't elect the Governor.

questions.stem: The RBI's primary objective under the amended RBI Act (post-2016) is to:

options.option_text: Maximise the Government's annual fiscal revenue
Maintain price stability while keeping growth in mind
Direct subsidised credit to all priority sectors
Manage the public debt-to-GDP ratio of the country

questions.explanation: RBI Act amendment (2016) — formalised FLEXIBLE INFLATION TARGETING (FIT). Primary objective: maintain PRICE STABILITY (CPI inflation 4% ± 2%, i.e. 2-6% band) while keeping in mind the OBJECTIVE OF GROWTH. Earlier 'multiple indicators' approach replaced. Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) operationalises this. Distractor 1 — fiscal revenue is the Centre's domain (CBDT, CBIC). Distractor 3 — priority-sector lending is a subsidiary objective. Distractor 4 — debt management is shared with Centre but not the PRIMARY objective.
